title: Log Aggregation with Loki & Grafana
summary: Logs from hundreds of pods across a cluster need to be centrally collected, stored, and queried. Loki (the 'Prometheus for logs') is already running in this cluster as part of the kube-prometheus-stack. Unlike Elasticsearch, Loki indexes only labels (not the full text), making it cheap to run. Grafana is the query frontend. This lesson covers Loki's architecture, LogQL (the query language), structured logging best practices, and how to build log dashboards in Grafana.

sections.title: Why log aggregation? The limits of kubectl logs
sections.body:
**`kubectl logs` breaks down at scale:**

```
kubectl logs <pod>          — works fine for one pod
kubectl logs -l app=web     — multi-pod, but truncated and slow
kubectl logs --previous     — only the immediately previous container
```

Problems that kubectl logs cannot solve:

```
1. Pod is gone  — OOMKilled, evicted, scaled down → logs are gone too
2. Scale        — 50 replicas of the same app → 50 kubectl logs calls
3. History      — default buffer is 10MB per container; older logs are evicted
4. Search       — no full-text search, no aggregation, no filters
5. Correlation  — can't join logs from frontend + backend + database
6. Alerting     — can't fire an alert when ERROR rate exceeds a threshold
```

**The aggregation stack:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Kubernetes Pods (stdout/stderr)                        │
│        │                                                │
│        ▼                                                │
│  Log collector (Promtail / Fluent Bit)                  │
│  Runs as DaemonSet — reads /var/log/containers/*.log    │
│        │                                                │
│        ▼                                                │
│  Loki  (storage + indexing by labels)                   │
│        │                                                │
│        ▼                                                │
│  Grafana  (query UI, dashboards, alerts)                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**This cluster already has this stack running:**

```bash
kubectl get pods -n monitoring | grep -E 'loki|promtail|grafana'
# loki-0                    1/1  Running
# promtail-xxxxx            1/1  Running  (one per node)
# grafana-xxxxxxxx          1/1  Running
```

sections.title: Loki architecture and label model
sections.body:
**Loki's core design principle: index labels, not content:**

```
Elasticsearch: indexes every word in every log line → expensive, fast full-text search
Loki:          indexes only stream labels → cheap, queries require label selection first
```

**Log streams — the unit of storage in Loki:**

A log stream is a set of log entries that share the same label set. Promtail automatically creates streams from Kubernetes metadata:

```
Stream 1: {namespace="production", pod="web-abc123", container="nginx"}
Stream 2: {namespace="production", pod="web-def456", container="nginx"}
Stream 3: {namespace="monitoring", pod="prometheus-0", container="prometheus"}
```

**Promtail — the log shipper:**

Promtail runs as a DaemonSet. For each node it:
1. Tails `/var/log/containers/*.log`
2. Enriches each line with Kubernetes metadata (namespace, pod, container, labels)
3. Applies relabeling rules
4. Ships to Loki

```yaml
# Promtail config (simplified)
clients:
  - url: http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: kubernetes-pods
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      # Use namespace and pod name as stream labels
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
        target_label: namespace
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_name]
        target_label: pod
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_name]
        target_label: container
      # Include pod labels as Loki labels (be selective — high cardinality = slow)
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
        target_label: app
```

**High cardinality warning:**

```
# BAD: pod IP as a label — millions of unique values
{pod_ip="10.244.1.42"}

# BAD: request ID as a label — unbounded cardinality
{request_id="uuid-xxxx"}

# GOOD: low-cardinality labels (dozens of unique values)
{namespace="production", app="checkout", env="prod"}

# Put high-cardinality values IN the log line, not as labels
# Log: {"level":"error","request_id":"abc","user_id":"42","msg":"payment failed"}
# Filter with LogQL: {app="checkout"} |= "payment failed" | json | user_id="42"
```

**Loki retention and storage:**

```yaml
# Loki config — data retention
limits_config:
  retention_period: 30d      # Delete logs older than 30 days

# Storage backends:
#   filesystem (default, single-node)
#   S3 / GCS / Azure Blob (production distributed)
#   MinIO (self-hosted S3-compatible)
```

sections.title: LogQL — querying logs
sections.body:
**LogQL is Loki's query language — inspired by PromQL:**

Every LogQL query starts with a log stream selector (like PromQL metric selectors):

```logql
# All logs from the production namespace
{namespace="production"}

# Logs from a specific app across all namespaces
{app="checkout"}

# Logs from a pod name matching a regex
{pod=~"web-.*"}

# Exclude a container
{namespace="production", container!="sidecar"}
```

**Log pipeline — filter and transform:**

```logql
# Filter by string (case-sensitive)
{app="checkout"} |= "ERROR"

# Exclude lines matching a pattern
{app="checkout"} != "health check"

# Regex filter
{app="checkout"} |~ "timeout|connection refused"

# Case-insensitive filter
{app="checkout"} |~ "(?i)error"
```

**Parsing structured logs:**

```logql
# Parse JSON log lines and filter on a parsed field
{app="checkout"} | json | level="error"

# Parse logfmt (key=value format)
{app="checkout"} | logfmt | status_code="500"

# Parse nginx access logs with pattern
{app="nginx"} | pattern `<ip> - - [<_>] "<method> <path> <_>" <status> <_>`
              | status >= 500

# Extract a field and use it in the pipeline
{app="checkout"} | json | line_format "{{.level}} {{.msg}}"
```

**Metric queries — aggregate log data:**

```logql
# Count error log rate per minute
rate({app="checkout"} |= "ERROR" [1m])

# Count HTTP 5xx errors by pod
sum by (pod) (
  rate({app="nginx"} | json | status >= 500 [5m])
)

# P99 latency from parsed log field (duration in ms)
quantile_over_time(0.99,
  {app="checkout"} | json | unwrap duration_ms [5m]
) by (pod)

# Error rate as percentage
sum(rate({app="checkout"} |= "ERROR" [5m]))
/
sum(rate({app="checkout"} [5m]))
* 100
```

**Useful LogQL patterns:**

```logql
# Find all pods that logged an OOMKill in the last hour
{namespace=~".+"} |= "OOMKilled"

# Recent errors from all apps, newest first
{namespace="production"} | json | level="error" | line_format "[{{.pod}}] {{.msg}}"

# Count unique users from access logs
count_over_time(
  {app="api"} | json | user_id != "" [1h]
) by (user_id)
```

sections.title: Structured logging best practices
sections.body:
**Structured logs are machine-parseable — always use JSON in production:**

```python
# Bad: unstructured log
print(f"Payment failed for user {user_id}: {error}")
# Log: Payment failed for user 42: connection timeout
# → Can grep for it, but can't easily aggregate by user_id or error type

# Good: structured JSON log
import logging
import json

class JSONFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        log = {
            "ts": self.formatTime(record),
            "level": record.levelname.lower(),
            "msg": record.getMessage(),
            "logger": record.name,
        }
        if hasattr(record, 'extra'):
            log.update(record.extra)
        if record.exc_info:
            log["exception"] = self.formatException(record.exc_info)
        return json.dumps(log)

# Usage:
logger.error("Payment failed", extra={"user_id": 42, "error": "connection timeout", "amount": 99.99})
# Log: {"ts":"2026-05-13T...","level":"error","msg":"Payment failed","user_id":42,...}
```

**Standard fields every log line should have:**

```json
{
  "ts": "2026-05-13T10:23:45.123Z",  // ISO 8601, always UTC
  "level": "error",                    // debug | info | warn | error
  "msg": "Payment processing failed",  // human-readable summary
  "service": "checkout",               // which service
  "trace_id": "abc123",               // correlates logs ↔ traces
  "span_id": "def456",
  "user_id": "42",                     // relevant business entity
  "request_id": "req-789",            // correlates a single request
  "duration_ms": 1234,                // for latency analysis
  "error": "connection timeout"        // machine-readable error type
}
```

**Log levels — use them correctly:**

```
DEBUG   — verbose development info, never in production (too noisy)
INFO    — normal operation events (request received, job completed)
WARN    — unexpected but recoverable (retry attempt, degraded mode)
ERROR   — something failed and needs attention (payment failed, DB down)
FATAL   — application cannot continue, about to exit
```

**Grafana Explore — querying Loki:**

```
1. Open Grafana (port 3001 in this lab)
2. Go to Explore (compass icon)
3. Select Loki as data source
4. Use the label browser or type LogQL directly
5. Switch between Logs and Metrics view
6. Click a log line → expand → see all parsed fields

Tip: set time range to "Last 15 minutes" for faster queries
Tip: use "Live" mode to tail logs in real time (like kubectl logs -f)
```

sections.title: Exercise: query cluster logs with LogQL
sections.body:
Use LogQL in Grafana to explore real logs from the running cluster.

```bash
# ── 1. Port-forward Grafana ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# (already done by start.sh grafana-ui — check if port 3001 is forwarded)
kubectl get svc -n monitoring | grep grafana

# If not already forwarded:
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/grafana 3001:80 &

# Open http://localhost:3001
# Default credentials: admin / prom-operator

# ── 2. Generate some logs to query ───────────────────────────────────────
# Deploy a pod that produces structured logs
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: log-generator
  labels:
    app: log-generator
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      i=0
      while true; do
        echo "{\"ts\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\",\"level\":\"info\",\"msg\":\"Request processed\",\"request_id\":\"req-$i\",\"duration_ms\":$((RANDOM % 500))}"
        if [ $((i % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then
          echo "{\"ts\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\",\"level\":\"error\",\"msg\":\"Connection failed\",\"request_id\":\"req-$i\",\"error\":\"timeout\"}"
        fi
        i=$((i+1))
        sleep 1
      done
EOF

# ── 3. Wait 30 seconds for Promtail to pick up the logs ──────────────────
sleep 30

# ── 4. Query logs from the terminal with Loki API directly ───────────────
# Get recent logs from the log-generator pod
curl -s -G \
  'http://loki.monitoring:3100/loki/api/v1/query_range' \
  --data-urlencode 'query={app="log-generator"}' \
  --data-urlencode 'limit=20' \
  --data-urlencode 'start=0' | python3 -m json.tool 2>/dev/null | head -50

# ── 5. Try LogQL queries in Grafana Explore ──────────────────────────────
# Paste each of these in Grafana Explore → Loki:

# All logs from log-generator:
# {app="log-generator"}

# Only errors:
# {app="log-generator"} |= "error"

# Parse JSON and filter on level field:
# {app="log-generator"} | json | level="error"

# Count error rate:
# rate({app="log-generator"} | json | level="error" [1m])

# ── 6. Query kube-system logs ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Find any OOMKill events in the cluster:
kubectl get events -A | grep OOMKill || echo 'No OOMKills yet'

# In Grafana Explore:
# {namespace="kube-system"} |= "error" | json

# ── 7. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete pod log-generator -n learning
```

questions.q: What is the key architectural difference between Loki and Elasticsearch for log storage?
options: Loki stores logs in S3 while Elasticsearch uses local disk
Loki indexes only stream labels, not full log content — making it much cheaper to run
Loki only supports JSON logs while Elasticsearch handles any format
Elasticsearch supports LogQL while Loki uses SQL
questions.explanation: Loki's core design: index labels (low-cardinality metadata like namespace, app, pod) but NOT the log content. This dramatically reduces storage and compute costs. Queries require a label selector first, then filter the log content in-query. Elasticsearch inverts every word, enabling faster full-text search but at much higher cost.

questions.q: Why is using `pod_ip` as a Loki label a problem?
options: IP addresses cannot be stored as label values
It creates high cardinality — millions of unique label values — making Loki slow and expensive
Pod IPs are only available after the pod starts
Promtail does not have access to pod IP addresses
questions.explanation: High cardinality labels (IPs, request IDs, user IDs, UUIDs) create massive numbers of unique log streams. Loki must maintain an index entry per unique label set — high cardinality makes this index huge, slowing queries and consuming memory. Put high-cardinality values in the log line itself, not as stream labels.

questions.q: What does the `| json` parser do in a LogQL query?
options: Converts the output to JSON format for the API response
Parses each log line as JSON and makes its fields available for filtering and formatting
Filters out any lines that are not valid JSON
Compresses the log data using JSON encoding
questions.explanation: `| json` is a log pipeline stage that parses each log line as a JSON object and extracts its top-level fields as labels for the remainder of the pipeline. This lets you then filter on `level="error"` or format output with `line_format` using extracted fields.

sections.title: Challenge: build a log dashboard in Grafana
sections.goal: Create a Grafana dashboard with three panels monitoring log activity across the cluster: an error rate graph, a log volume by namespace, and a live log tail panel for a specific application.
hints: In Grafana, go to Dashboards → New → New Dashboard → Add visualization, then select Loki as the data source
For error rate: use `sum(rate({namespace=~".+"} |= "error" [5m])) by (namespace)` — switch panel type to Time series
For log volume: use `sum(rate({namespace=~".+"} [5m])) by (namespace)` as a stacked bar chart
For the live log tail: use a Logs panel type (not Time series) with a LogQL log query, and enable live mode
Save the dashboard and set the refresh interval to 30s
success_criteria: Dashboard has at least 3 panels using Loki as data source
At least one panel uses a metric query (rate/sum) — displayed as Time series
At least one panel uses a log query — displayed as Logs panel type
Dashboard is saved and visible in the Grafana dashboard list
